issues.legal_issue: A conviction for murder may be sustained on circumstantial evidence when the proved circumstances form a complete chain pointing to guilt, including where an accused who shared a home with the deceased and was last seen with the deceased gives no reasonable explanation for the death or disappearance.
material_facts: The deceased lived in the same house as the accused and her children.
The deceased’s son testified that the accused beat the deceased and took her away from the house; the deceased was later found dead in a forest.
The autopsy evidence established that the deceased’s injuries were ante-mortem and that hanging occurred after death.
The accused did not report the deceased missing and offered no reasonable explanation for her death.
The prosecution evidence established motive and the other circumstances that the Court found cumulatively formed a complete chain pointing to the accused’s guilt.
issues.conclusion: The circumstances formed a complete chain establishing the accused’s guilt, and the murder conviction was affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: In a case based on circumstantial evidence, the circumstances must be cogently and firmly established, point unerringly to guilt, form a complete chain, and be inconsistent with innocence. Under Section 106 of the Evidence Act, an accused who was an inmate of the home and was last seen with the deceased must explain facts especially within his knowledge; failure to give a reasonable explanation is a strong incriminating circumstance when considered with the prosecution evidence. The Court relied on Trimukh Maroti Kirkan v. State of Maharashtra (2006) 10 SCC 681; State of Rajasthan v. Kashi Ram (2006) 12 SCC 254; Ganesh Lal v. State of Rajasthan (2002) 1 SCC 731; State of Maharashtra v. Suresh (2000) 1 SCC 471; and State of Tamil Nadu v. Rajendran (1999) 8 SCC 679.

rule.if: circumstantial_murder_case and deceased_shared_home_with_accused and deceased_last_seen_with_accused and homicidal_death_established and accused_failed_to_report_disappearance and accused_offered_no_reasonable_explanation and prosecution_established_complete_chain

predicates.circumstantial_murder_case: The prosecution seeks to establish a murder charge through circumstantial evidence.
predicates.deceased_shared_home_with_accused: The deceased lived in the same home as the accused.
predicates.deceased_last_seen_with_accused: The deceased was last seen alive in the accused’s company.
predicates.homicidal_death_established: Evidence established that the deceased died through a homicidal act.
predicates.accused_failed_to_report_disappearance: The accused did not report the deceased’s disappearance to the authorities.
predicates.accused_offered_no_reasonable_explanatio: The accused gave no reasonable explanation for the deceased’s death or disappearance.
predicates.prosecution_established_complete_chain: The prosecution established circumstances that cumulatively formed a complete chain pointing to the accused’s guilt and inconsistent with innocence.

issues.definition: When a circumstantial murder prosecution establishes the listed circumstances and a complete chain pointing to guilt, the murder conviction is upheld.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s testimony must be assessed as a whole and in its circumstances, and improvements or omissions do not alone make it unreliable when the testimony is otherwise natural, cogent, and consistent with the prosecution case.
material_facts: The deceased’s son lived with the deceased and the accused and was a natural witness to the events.
He testified that he heard his mother’s cries and saw the accused take her away, and that he was threatened afterward.
His initial statement did not name two other alleged participants, and the High Court treated improvements and omissions as reasons to reject his evidence.
The trial court had observed the witness’s demeanour and found his evidence trustworthy; the Supreme Court noted his age, fear, and the circumstances in which his initial statement was made.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in rejecting the witness’s evidence on the ground of alleged improvements; the evidence was credible in the circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: A witness’s evidence must first be read as a whole to determine whether it appears truthful in the circumstances; identified drawbacks and infirmities must then be assessed against the general tenor of the prosecution case. A natural and cogent account is not rendered unreliable merely by an omission or improvement, particularly when the circumstances explain it.

rule.if: appeal_from_acquittal and witness_was_natural_observer and witness_account_was_cogent_and_consistent and omission_or_improvement_had_contextual_explanation

predicates.appeal_from_acquittal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging an acquittal.
predicates.witness_was_natural_observer: The witness was present by reason of ordinary circumstances and was positioned to observe or hear relevant events.
predicates.witness_account_was_cogent_and_consisten: The witness’s account was coherent and consistent with the prosecution case when considered as a whole.
predicates.omission_or_improvement_had_contextual_e: The circumstances, including fear or distress, explained the omission or difference in the witness’s earlier account.

issues.definition: When a natural observer gives a cogent and consistent account and the circumstances explain an omission or improvement, the testimony is accepted as reliable.
